title: Yo Yo Honey Singh Reveals Gajar Ka Halwa Is the Indian Sweet He Can Never Refuse
excerpt: In a rapid-fire interview with AB Talks, the rapper and singer named the Mughal-era carrot dessert as his all-time weakness — and a simple recipe shows why diaspora kitchens keep it alive year-round.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Yo Yo Honey Singh's favorite Indian dessert is gajar ka halwa, a classic carrot pudding.
  • Gajar ka halwa originated in Mughal kitchens, evolving with the introduction of orange carrots in the 17th century.
  • Nutritionists recommend limiting gajar ka halwa to half a cup due to its high calorie content.
  • A quick recipe by Tan France allows making gajar ka halwa in under 40 minutes using evaporated milk.

When Yo Yo Honey Singh sat down for a rapid-fire round with the popular interview series AB Talks, the Punjabi rapper did not hesitate when asked to name the one Indian dessert he can "never say no" to.

"Gajar ka halwa," he said — and millions of fans across India and its diaspora likely nodded in agreement.

A Mughal-Era Classic That Endures

Gajar ka halwa, also known as gajrela in parts of North India, is a slow-cooked carrot pudding enriched with milk, sugar, ghee and cardamom. The dessert traces its origins to the Mughal period, according to food historian Colleen Taylor Sen, who writes in Feasts and Fasts that halwa arrived in India with the Delhi Sultanate between the 13th and 16th centuries.

The carrot variant came later. Food columnist Rajaysree Sen has noted that Dutch farmers developed orange carrots in the 17th century as a tribute to William of Orange. Those carrots traveled through Afghanistan to Punjab, where home cooks began grating them into milk on coal stoves — and gajar ka halwa was born.

> **"Add a quarter cup of granulated sugar and cook until dissolved."**

Today, the dessert is synonymous with North Indian winters, appearing at Diwali gatherings, wedding feasts and family dinners from Delhi to Ludhiana — and increasingly, in diaspora kitchens from New Jersey to London.

"Women cooked gajar ka halwa for hours on coal stoves, waiting for the grated carrot to cook through while the milk it was cooking in halved its quantity. Now people use khoya, milk solids available in sweet shops, instead of milk, to save time."

— Rajaysree Sen, food columnist

The Nutrition Tradeoff

The halwa is not without its caveats. Edwina Raj, Head of Clinical Nutrition & Dietetics at Aster CMI Hospital in Bangalore, told The Madras Pulse that while carrots bring vitamins, minerals and fiber, the traditional preparation is loaded with sugar and saturated fat.

Raj recommends diabetics enjoy the dish only occasionally in small portions, and suggests reducing added sugar in favor of the carrots' natural sweetness. Swapping full-fat milk for a low-fat version and cutting back on ghee can trim calories, she adds, while almonds or walnuts boost satiety with healthy fats.

A Quick Recipe for Diaspora Kitchens

Gajar Ka Halwa: A Historical Delight
›Originated in Mughal kitchens between the 13th and 16th centuries.
›Carrots introduced by Dutch farmers in the 17th century.
›Traditional preparation involves slow cooking on coal stoves.
›Gajar ka halwa is a winter staple in North India and diaspora kitchens.

For those inspired to try it at home, Queer Eye star Tan France — himself of South Asian heritage — has shared a streamlined version on Instagram that takes under 40 minutes.

The method: grate four to five large carrots and sauté them in one tablespoon of ghee for five to seven minutes. Add a quarter cup of granulated sugar and cook until dissolved. Pour in one and a half cans of evaporated milk and simmer for 15 to 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the milk is absorbed and the mixture thickens. Fold in ground cardamom and raisins, cook five more minutes, then finish with coarse brown sugar if desired. Garnish with chopped pistachios.

The evaporated milk shortcut bypasses the hours-long reduction that traditional recipes demand — a practical swap for weeknight cooking in diaspora households where time is short but nostalgia runs deep.

"Add a quarter cup of granulated sugar and cook until dissolved."

From Street Stalls to Instagram Feeds

Gajar ka halwa has seen a resurgence beyond home kitchens. The dessert regularly trends on Indian food Instagram, with home chefs and restaurants posting artful bowls garnished with edible silver leaf, saffron threads and crushed pistachios. In the US and UK, Indian restaurants have added it to winter menus, sometimes served warm alongside a scoop of vanilla ice cream.

Quick Recipe for Diaspora Kitchens
›Grate 4-5 large carrots.
›Sauté in 1 tablespoon of ghee for 5-7 minutes.
›Add 1/4 cup sugar and dissolve.
›Pour in 1.5 cans of evaporated milk and simmer for 15-20 minutes.
›Finish with cardamom, raisins, and optional brown sugar.

For Honey Singh, whose career has spanned chart-topping hits like Blue Eyes and Desi Kalakaar, the choice carries a simpler meaning. It is the taste of Punjab, of winters spent at home — a flavor that fame and travel have not dulled.

The next time red carrots appear at your local Indian grocery store, consider channeling the rapper's enthusiasm. A pot, some ghee, and 40 minutes of patience are all it takes.
